$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E,B$ be the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and
$\rho,J$ the source fields of [[def-em-sources]], with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and
$\rho,J$ of class $C^1$, and suppose the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds with these fields and sources, in particular
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Then the continuity equation

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$$

holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, where $\operatorname{div}$ is the
divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
$\partial_t$ the partial time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(b) [Distributional branch] Let $E,B,\rho,J$ be distributions on
$\Omega\times I$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]); in
particular they may be locally integrable fields and sources identified with
their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Suppose the four
equations

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$ with distributional derivatives. This
includes the original locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and the separately adopted declared singular-source
models of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], when their source and
field hypotheses hold. More generally the formal compatibility implication
applies to every distributional source pair for which the four identities
hold, without asserting physical adoption of arbitrary distributions. Then
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$.

The conclusion is a compatibility condition: it does not assert that every
source pair is compatible with the Maxwell equations, and by itself it proves
no conservation of physical charge. The derivative compatibility argument is
choice-free. An application to the declared singular-source model retains the
Countable Choice assumption of its defining source and surface-measure
formulation ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of the
imported piecewise $C^1$ boundary and surface-measure definitions
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let
$E,B$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$; and let $(V,\nu_V)$ and $(D,r)$ be the
volume and patch test geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]. Assume the
fields are jointly $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ and that the additional
derivatives appearing below exist and are continuous there; for instance $E,B$
jointly of class $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ is sufficient.

(a) [Differential implies integral] If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, then for every
volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$ and every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0,$$

and for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions
$t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and
$t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for
every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS,\qquad \oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS.$$

(b) [Integral implies differential] Conversely, suppose the two volume
identities of (a) hold for every volume test geometry and every $t\in I$, and
that for every patch test geometry the two flux functions are differentiable
on $I$ and the two patch identities of (a) hold for every $t\in I$. Then the
four smooth-branch equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

The equivalence is asserted for the exact class of test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], which contains the open interiors of all closed
axis-parallel boxes compactly contained in $\Omega$ and the affine square
patches; it is not a recovery from one selected volume or one selected patch,
and the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are the operators used.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

A **$C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region** is a regular parametrized surface patch $(D,\varphi)$ in the sense of [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]] whose parameter region $D$ is supplied, in addition, with a decomposition making it a finite elementary Green region in the sense of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], and whose parametrization $\varphi$ is of class $C^2$ on an open neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Both requirements on $D$ are part of the data: it is a compact Jordan parameter region, so it is the closure of its nonempty connected interior, and it carries a supplied elementary decomposition.

Let $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ be the positive boundary chain of that decomposition, the finite list of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs of [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]. Then the **induced boundary chain** is the list of arcs obtained by composing the positive boundary chain of the parameter region with the parametrization, namely

$$\varphi(\partial D):=(\varphi\circ\sigma_1,\ldots,\varphi\circ\sigma_m),$$

each entry a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $\mathbb R^3$ in the sense of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]]. For a continuous vector field $F$ on a set containing $\varphi[D]$, the **circulation of $F$ around the induced boundary chain** is the finite sum

$$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{l=1}^m\int_{\varphi\circ\sigma_l}F\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

with the vector line integrals of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. The value does not depend on the order of the list, a finite sum of reals being independent of its order.

If instead $F$ is defined on an open set $U$ containing $\varphi[D]$, continuity of $\varphi$ and compactness of $D$ give an open neighbourhood $V$ of $D$ in the domain of $\varphi$ with $\varphi[V]\subseteq U$. On $V$, the **pulled-back functions** are the inner products of the field along the parametrization with the two parameter derivatives:

$$P^{*}:=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle,\qquad Q^{*}:=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle,$$

with the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The oriented area vector $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v$ and the flux it computes are those of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. A merely continuous field on an arbitrary set containing $\varphi[D]$ is enough for circulation, but not for these neighbourhood-defined pullbacks.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention
already carried by the imported finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentations
and by the compact $C^1$ surface measure cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ open and
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval. This definition fixes the
time-independent spatial test geometries of the integral form of the Maxwell
equations.

(a) [Volume test geometry] A **volume test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a pair
$(V,\nu_V)$ where $V\subseteq\Omega$ is a nonempty bounded open set with
$\overline V\subseteq\Omega$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
of its boundary ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), and
$\nu_V$ is the outward unit normal of that presentation off its edge set
([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]). The
**closed-surface flux** of a field $F$ continuous on a neighbourhood of
$\overline V$ is the finite face sum

$$\oint_{\partial V}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS,$$

with the face surface integrals of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. For every closed
axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$, its
open interior $V=\prod_{i<3}(a_i,b_i)$ is a volume test geometry and
$\overline V=K$; its natural six-face presentation is the boundary of $K$, with
outward normals $\pm e_i$. The volume variable is $V$, while $K$ denotes its
compact closure. Each face is a degenerate three-dimensional box and hence has
$\lambda_3$-measure zero by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]; their finite union
$K\setminus V$ is null. Thus for continuous $h$ on a neighbourhood of $K$,
$\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3=\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$: the positive and negative integrals
over the null difference vanish by
[[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

(b) [Patch test geometry] A **patch test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a regular
$C^2$ surface patch $(D,r)$ over a finite elementary Green region in the sense
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]],
[[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]): $D\subseteq\mathbb
R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r$ is of class $C^2$ on an open
neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
$r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) and
no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$. Its
**induced boundary chain** $\partial S=r(\partial D)$ and its **circulation**
$\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ for a field continuous on the image are
those of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]); its
**oriented flux** of a field $F$ continuous on the image is

$$\int_SF\cdot n_S\,dS:=\int_D(F\circ r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)\,dudv,$$

the scalar Riemann integral of the continuous integrand on the compact Jordan
parameter region, in the orientation induced by $r$
([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). The pair $(D,r)$
is part of the data. Every affine graph patch $r(u,v)=(u,v,\varphi(u,v))$ over
an axis-parallel square $D=[c_1,c_1+\ell]\times[c_2,c_2+\ell]$ with $\ell>0$,
whose graph lies in $\Omega$ with $\varphi$ affine (for instance constant), and
more generally every affine regular patch over such a square, is a patch test
geometry: the square is a finite elementary Green region, and $r$ is smooth and
regular with $\varphi_u,\varphi_v$ constant.

(c) [Regularity convention] When an integral identity of this framework is
asserted for a volume test geometry $V$, respectively for a patch test geometry
$S$, with respect to a field $F$ of stated class $C^k$, it concerns fields
defined and of class $C^k$ on an open neighbourhood of $\overline V$ in
$\Omega$, respectively of the image $r[D]$ in $\Omega$; when the identity
involves a time derivative of a flux, the field is defined with the stated
regularity on a neighbourhood of that compact set times the compact time
interval of the assertion. No regularity away from these neighbourhoods is
asserted.

(d) [Conventions and scope] Test geometries are fixed spatial subsets of
$\Omega$ and carry no motion. A patch's orientation is the one induced by its
parametrization, and its induced boundary chain has the compatible orientation
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], so that the
classical Stokes theorem applies with a plus sign. The definition retains the
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the imported boundary and surface-measure
definitions; it asserts no differential equation, no physical law and no
existence of fields.

A compact **Type I region** is

$$D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \alpha(x)\le y\le\beta(x)\},$$

where $a<b$, the continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy $\alpha\le\beta$, and $\alpha<\beta$ on $(a,b)$. A compact **Type II region** is defined analogously by continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\lambda\le\rho$ on $[c,d]$:

$$D=\{(x,y):c\le y\le d,\ \lambda(y)\le x\le\rho(y)\}.$$

An **elementary Green region** admits both descriptions. By [[thm-fubini-over-a-region-between-continuous-graphs]], each Type I description is compact and Jordan measurable.

A **finite elementary Green region** is a nonempty finite union $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ of elementary Green regions with pairwise disjoint interiors. Pairwise intersections must be finite unions of complete shared boundary arcs and endpoints, and every positive-length internal arc must belong to exactly two pieces with opposite induced orientations. This supplied decomposition is part of the data; it is not inferred from an arbitrary closed curve.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge1$ there is a fixed smooth $b:\mathbb R^n\to[0,1]$, equal to one on $\overline B_1(0)$ and with support contained in $B_2(0)$. For $a\in\mathbb R^n,r>0$, $b_{a,r}(x)=b((x-a)/r)$ satisfies $\int|Db_{a,r}|=C_nr^{n-1}$, where $C_n=\int|Db|<\infty$. For every $0<r<R$ one can instead obtain a smooth bump equal to one on $\overline B_r(a)$ and supported strictly inside $B_R(a)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

derivations.claim: Put $G:=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$, a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of $\overline V$ by the regularity of the data. The Gauss law, commutation of mixed partials and the smooth continuity identity give $\operatorname{div}G=\operatorname{div}J+\varepsilon_0\partial_t\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho=0$ there; applying the divergence theorem to $G$ on the specified presentation of $V$, whose faces are $S_1,S_2$ with outward normals $-n_1,+n_2$, gives $0=\int_V\operatorname{div}G=\int_{S_2}G\cdot n_2\,dS-\int_{S_1}G\cdot n_1\,dS$, which is the first asserted equality of (a). For the second equality, the integral Ampere identity applies to either patch; since both induced boundary chains are the same oriented loop $\gamma$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE\cdot n\,dS=\int_S\partial_tE\cdot n\,dS$ on a fixed patch, the identity reads $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_{S_i}(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE)\cdot n_i\,dS$ for $i=1,2$, because $c^{-2}/\mu_0=\varepsilon_0$; dividing by $\mu_0>0$ gives the stated value.

For (c), verify the smooth equations by direct substitution: $\operatorname{div}E=(t/\varepsilon_0)\chi'(z)$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$; $\operatorname{curl}(E_z(z,t)e_z)=0$ because $E_z$ is independent of the first two coordinates, so $\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$; $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ and $\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE=-\mu_0\chi(z)e_z+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\chi(z)e_z=0$ because $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$; and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=\chi'(z)-\chi'(z)=0$. For the standard smooth step the function $h(s)=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$ is smooth, equals one for $|s|\le1/\sqrt2$, is strictly positive for $|s|<1$ and vanishes for $|s|\ge1$; hence $\eta(u,v)=h(u)h(v)$ is a smooth compactly supported function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one near the origin, strictly positive on the open square $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$ and zero on and outside $\partial D$.

Splitting $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$ in the equality of step 1.1 and using linearity of the surface integrals in the integrand gives $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1-\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2=-\varepsilon_0(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE\cdot n_1-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE\cdot n_2)$, which is (b); in particular the two conduction fluxes are equal exactly when the two displacement fluxes are, and the Maxwell equations alone force neither equality.

For (c), the graphs $r_1(u,v)=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v))$ and $r_2(u,v)=(u,v,0)$ have parameter derivatives with cross products $r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v}=(2\eta_u,2\eta_v,1)$ and $r_{2,u}\times r_{2,v}=e_z$, both nonzero on the interior of $D$; the boundary chains take values $(u,v,0)$ on $\partial D$ for both, so they coincide, and the region $V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,-2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is bounded, open, nonempty, and has exactly the two graph faces with outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ off the square seam, which is a finite union of line segments of surface measure zero; thus the presentation hypotheses of [F2] are met. The oriented flux formula gives $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_D(J\circ r_1)\cdot(r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v})\,dudv=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv$ and $\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0$. On $Q_0=[-1/2,1/2]^2$ we have $\eta=1$ and $\chi(-2\eta)=1$. The integrand is nonnegative on $D$; cutting $D$ along the four sides of $Q_0$, coordinate-slice additivity and monotonicity [F5] give $\int_D\chi(-2\eta)\ge\int_{Q_0}1=1$, where the constant integral is its constant Darboux-sum value. Hence the first flux is strictly negative, while the second vanishes; the total fluxes vanish because $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE=-\chi(z)e_z+\chi(z)e_z=0$, consistently with $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (a) and (b) under the stated hypotheses, and steps 1.2 and 2.2 verify that the declared smooth slab data satisfy every hypothesis of (a) and (b) with $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS<0=\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS$, so the conduction-only flux genuinely depends on the spanning surface while the total current flux does not; the construction is a conditional model computation, the capacitor reading is explanatory, and no measurement or thin-wire source is claimed.
